title: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College; Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina
lead: A membership organization challenges two admissions systems through different appellate routes; the Court first accepts its representative standing and then reverses both judgments.

actors.name: Students for Fair Admissions (SFFA)
actors.role: Nonprofit membership organization challenging race-conscious admissions.

actors.name: Harvard College
actors.role: Private, federally funded college sued under Title VI.

actors.name: University of North Carolina (UNC)
actors.role: Public university sued under the Fourteenth Amendment.

proceedings: Separate district courts upheld Harvard’s and UNC’s admissions programs after trials.
The First Circuit affirmed Harvard; the Supreme Court took UNC before appellate judgment.
The Supreme Court reversed the First Circuit and the Middle District of North Carolina in distinct judgments.
limits: The 2023 votes were 6–2 in Harvard and 6–3 in UNC because Jackson took no part in Harvard. Military-academy admissions and subsequent applications were not decided. Pinpoints are original slip-opinion pages.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Two universities consider race within different admissions systems
paragraphs: Harvard College, a private institution receiving federal funds, used several admissions stages. Initial readers scored academic, extracurricular, athletic, school-support, personal, and overall qualities; race could affect the overall rating. Regional subcommittees recommended applicants to roughly forty full-committee members, who discussed racial composition and voted individually. A final reduction called the lop identified legacy, recruited-athlete, financial-aid, and race information. The trial court found race a determinative tip for a significant share of admitted African-American and Hispanic applicants.

The University of North Carolina (UNC), a public institution, used readers to rate multiple dimensions and recommend decisions. Race could supply a substantial plus in individual cases. Most recommendations were provisionally final, but a school-group committee reviewed every decision and could also consider race. The later Court and dissents drew different inferences from these findings and statistics; their descriptions are not unanimous factual conclusions.

Students for Fair Admissions (SFFA), a nonprofit formed in 2014 to defend civil rights and equal protection, sued both in November 2014. Harvard’s case invoked Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; UNC’s included the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. Harvard’s trial ran fifteen days with thirty witnesses, UNC’s eight days. Both district courts upheld the programs. The First Circuit affirmed Harvard. The Supreme Court granted ordinary certiorari there and certiorari before judgment in UNC, where no Fourth Circuit merits judgment existed. The schools defended individualized review and diversity’s educational benefits, arguing that available race-neutral alternatives would not adequately preserve their missions; SFFA sought abandonment of permissive precedent and alternatively disputed narrow tailoring.

sources.pinpoint: Admissions systems and litigation; Court 2–6; Sotomayor 27–35

sections.title: UNC questions whether SFFA truly represents members
sections.cue: How did Hunt apply to an ordinary voluntary association?
paragraphs: Before the merits, UNC argued that SFFA was not a genuine membership organization at filing because members did not control and fund it. Article III requires injury, traceability, and redressability. Under Hunt, an association can represent members who could sue individually, on interests germane to its purpose, when neither claim nor relief requires individual participation. The universities did not contest those three requirements; they proposed an additional governance condition.

Chief Justice Roberts’s opinion rejected that reading. Hunt concerned a state apple commission without conventional members. Growers’ and dealers’ control, service, and financing showed that they functioned as members. Those features substituted for formal membership; they were not further requirements for every voluntary association.

SFFA had identifiable voluntary members whom it represented in good faith. Harvard’s filing involved an incorporated nonprofit with forty-seven such members. UNC’s record identified four rejected applicants who joined, supported the mission, received updates, and could provide input. Additional operational scrutiny was unnecessary. The Court did not abolish Hunt’s three requirements, authorize representation without an injured member, or decide direct organizational injury. The assigned discussion’s neighboring Brown Group, Flyers Rights, and American Physicians material concerns other decisions.

sections.title: The majority applies strict scrutiny to both programs
sections.cue: Why did the universities’ objectives and classifications fail its review?
paragraphs: Roberts traced equal protection from Reconstruction through segregation and Brown and emphasized legal treatment of persons without racial distinction. Racial classifications require a compelling interest and narrow tailoring. The opinion identified remediation of specified unlawful discrimination and prevention of serious imminent prison violence as recognized interests elsewhere, without deciding all settings. Neither school defended its present program as remedying its own past discrimination.

Harvard was evaluated through precedent linking Title VI violations to equal-protection standards; no party sought reconsideration of that linkage. Federal funding did not turn Harvard into a public institution directly bound by the Fourteenth Amendment. Reviewing Bakke and Grutter, Roberts identified strict scrutiny, absence of racial negatives or stereotypes, and a meaningful endpoint as indispensable conditions. He found each lacking.

Goals such as leadership, citizenship, knowledge, empathy, and exchange of ideas were commendable but too unfocused and unmeasurable to determine necessary preferences or completion. Overbroad, undefined, or underinclusive racial categories weakened the fit between classification and educational goals. Academic deference could not replace judicial scrutiny.

The Court viewed finite admissions as zero-sum: racial advantages could reduce others’ opportunities even when described as positive factors. It also regarded preferences based on race itself as assuming group-linked perspectives contrary to individualized dignity and Grutter’s antistereotyping limit. Dissents disputed both the inferences and the portrayal of holistic review.

Neither program had a meaningful endpoint. Representation measures risked balancing, educational benefits lacked a definite completion point, and periodic reconsideration could not authorize indefinite preferences. Harvard’s year-to-year composition chart figured in that analysis and was differently understood by the dissent. Grutter’s twenty-five-year expectation did not permit otherwise unlawful treatment until 2028; neither university identified an actual end date.

sections.title: The concurrences offer additional reasons
sections.cue: Which propositions were specific to Thomas, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh?
paragraphs: Justice Thomas joined the Court and defended a colorblind constitutional account through Reconstruction laws, segregation history, statutory arguments, and remedial classifications. He rejected deference to universities’ claimed benefits and argued that preferences could generate mismatch, stigma, resentment, and reduced individuality. Sotomayor disputed those assertions; they were his arguments rather than empirical findings adopted across the Court. He viewed Grutter as effectively overruled and supported race-neutral opportunities.

Justice Gorsuch, joined by Thomas, read Title VI independently to prohibit a federal-funds recipient from intentionally treating a similarly situated person worse even partly because of race. His textual and but-for analysis associated with Bostock rejected benign motives, other contributing causes, or group-wide benefit as defenses. Liability did not require resolving every dispute over the preferences’ magnitude or motivation. He questioned equating differently worded constitutional and statutory provisions and criticized Bakke’s interpretive approach. Roberts retained the established linkage instead.

Justice Kavanaugh emphasized the temporary nature of permissible classifications and Grutter’s twenty-five-year expectation, including the approaching college class of 2028 and the absence of any defended later termination. He acknowledged ongoing discrimination and race-neutral ways to address its effects. His temporal account supplemented, rather than displaced, the majority’s finding that these programs already violated substantive limits.

sections.title: The dissents dispute the historical and practical account
sections.cue: Why did Sotomayor and Jackson think the programs should survive?
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor, joined by Kagan and by Jackson only in UNC, read Reconstruction, Brown, and admissions precedent as permitting limited race-conscious measures toward genuine equality after segregation. She emphasized academic freedom, educational benefits, trial findings, and the practical insufficiency of SFFA’s alternatives. She accused the majority of displacing precedent without necessary stare decisis and reliance analysis.

Sotomayor thought demanding measurable outcomes while condemning numerical attention created an impossible test. Individual essays largely described existing holistic review. She disputed statistical and stereotyping inferences, the portrayal of simple preferences, and uncertain termination requirements, warning of reduced diversity and professional pipelines.

Jackson’s UNC-only dissent, joined by Sotomayor and Kagan, described how law and policy transmitted wealth, educational, housing, and health disparities. John and James were illustrative hypothetical applicants, not parties. She characterized UNC’s forty-criteria process as individual review with voluntary racial disclosure, no quota, and no automatic racial plus, disagreeing with the majority’s inferences. Recognizing unequal opportunities, she argued, could improve assessment of merit and produce wider benefits, while mandatory race blindness perpetuated inequality. Her historical and empirical discussion remained dissenting analysis, not Court findings.

sections.title: Both judgments are reversed with express limits
sections.cue: What can still be considered about an applicant’s individual experience?
paragraphs: On June 29, 2023, the Court reversed the First Circuit judgment in Harvard and the Middle District of North Carolina judgment in UNC. Roberts wrote for himself, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett. Sotomayor and Kagan dissented in both; Jackson participated and dissented only in UNC. The votes were therefore six to two and six to three, even though one published instrument resolved both cases.

The majority allowed consideration of how race affected an applicant’s individual life, including discrimination or inspiration, when tied to courage, leadership, ability, or another personal quality. It barred essays or other devices used simply to reproduce the invalid preference system. The decision neither categorically prohibited mentioning race nor permitted a preference whenever an essay did so.

Military academies were not parties and could present distinct interests. Their reservation was not a holding that their practices were lawful. This account preserves the original judgments and reasoning, not a certification of later applications.
